title: SIRS and multiple organ dysfunction
definition: Complicated babesiosis is disease with signs that haemolytic anaemia alone does not explain, from one organ complication to failure of several organs [R1][R2]. SIRS is two or more of four criteria (temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, leukocytes); MODS is dysfunction of two or more organs [R3][R4].
definition_note: Working definition changed. SIRS and complicated disease are not the same thing. Most dogs with babesiosis meet the SIRS criteria, and SIRS did not predict death in B. rossi [R5][R3]. Complicated disease starts with one organ complication; MODS is the severe end. The 2026 canine sepsis consensus also puts organ dysfunction, not SIRS, at the centre of the definition [R6].
key_points: SIRS criteria are met by most dogs with B. rossi (61 to 87%) and many with B. canis (37 to 68%); in B. rossi, SIRS did not predict death [R5][R3][R4][R7].
Organ dysfunction predicts death. In B. canis, survival was 45% with two failing organs, 10% with three and 0% with four [R4].
On arrival, collapse, cerebral signs, haemoconcentration, hypoglycaemia, high urea or creatinine, high bilirubin and high lactate mark the B. rossi dogs that die [R3].
Most B. rossi deaths occur within 24 hours of admission, so triage and early referral matter [R3].
A lactate that does not fall by half in 8 to 16 hours was linked to death [R8].
No anti-inflammatory or immunomodulating drug has been shown to help in dogs. In human cerebral malaria, dexamethasone caused harm [R9][R10].

description.heading: What it is
description.text: South African authors first split dogs into 'severe' disease (life-threatening anaemia) and 'complicated' disease (complications not caused by the anaemia). Jacobson called this split artificial and proposed grading dogs by severity, using simple signs such as collapse and abnormal breathing [R1]. The terms follow the complicated and uncomplicated forms of falciparum malaria [R3]. The SIRS and MODS model was applied to B. rossi in 2001 and to B. canis in Croatia [R5][R4]. In the Zagreb B. canis studies, uncomplicated means no organ dysfunction, complicated means one or more, and MODS means two or more [R2]. The 2026 canine consensus defines sepsis as organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection [R6].

description.heading: How common, and in which dogs
description.text: B. rossi (Onderstepoort): SIRS in 87% of 91 complicated cases and MODS in 48% of 56 [R5]; SIRS in 61% of 266 dogs, and 34 of 320 dogs died or were euthanased [R3]. Mortality was 12% in admitted dogs [R1]. B. canis: SIRS in 68% of 332 dogs and MODS in 10% [R4]; SIRS in 59% of 54 dogs [R11] and 37% of 49 dogs in Germany [R7]. In Hungary, 31 of 63 dogs had complications, and old age was a risk factor for multiple complications [R12]. In 342 German dogs, 87.6% had an uncomplicated course and mortality was 6.7% [R13].

description.heading: When in the course of disease
description.text: Complications are usually present on arrival. In the Onderstepoort cohort, all treated dogs that died did so within 24 hours of admission [R3]. In a Zagreb series, dogs with septic shock died between day 1 and day 4 [R14]. Pro-inflammatory cytokines were higher in B. rossi dogs that came in within 48 hours of the first signs [R15].

description.heading: Mechanism
description.text: B. rossi provokes a mixed cytokine response; IL-6 and MCP-1 were higher in dogs that died [R15]. Jacobson argues that tissue hypoxia plays a major part beside inflammation [R1]. Dogs with a compromised circulation had higher parasitaemias and died more often, but parasite load is unlikely to be the only trigger [R16].

species_notes.note: The main species in South Africa and the most severe. Prognostic data come from a few Onderstepoort cohorts that may share dogs [R3][R8][R17].
Most SIRS and MODS counts, and the organ-count gradient, come from European clinics [R4][R11][R12][R7]. Mortality was 6.7% in a recent German series of 342 dogs [R13].
One Indian study derived an outcome score [R18]. The N-acetylcysteine trials were in outpatient B. gibsoni dogs, not in dogs with MODS [R19][R20].

criteria.threshold: 2 or more of: leukocytes above 12 or below 4 x10^9/L, or 10% or more band cells; rectal temperature below 37.8 or above 39.7 °C; heart rate 160/min or more; respiratory rate 40/min or more
criteria.note: Okano criteria as applied to 320 B. rossi dogs; nearly the same criteria in 49 B. canis dogs. Not predictive of death on its own.
Zagreb criteria, 40 B. canis dogs. In B. rossi, creatinine above 106 µmol/L was linked to death.

criteria.threshold: ALT above 176 U/L, ALP above 360 U/L and total bilirubin above 100 µmol/L

criteria.note: Zagreb criteria, B. canis. See SY15.

criteria.threshold: dyspnoea with typical nasal discharge, or pulmonary oedema on radiographs
criteria.note: Zagreb criteria, B. canis. See SY08.
Zagreb criteria, using the scale of Welzl et al. Exclude hypoglycaemia first.
Used in B. canis and B. rossi studies; the organ criteria differ between groups.

criteria.threshold: SIRS, then MODS, with hypotension that does not respond to treatment
criteria.note: Definition of one Zagreb case series; all 10 such dogs died.

criteria.threshold: unable to stand unaided on arrival
criteria.note: 22.5% of 320 B. rossi dogs; 24 of the 34 deaths were in collapsed dogs.

clinical_signs.note: Odds ratio for death 8.4 in B. rossi. Collapse was also the main risk factor for hypoglycaemia.

clinical_signs.sign: Cerebral signs (stupor, coma, seizures) with normal or high glucose
clinical_signs.note: 6 of 320 B. rossi dogs; all died. See SY07.
Proposed as a simple severity marker; pulmonary oedema marks lung dysfunction. See SY08.
The odds of death rose 1.4 times for each 1 °C fall in B. rossi.
21 of 100 B. rossi dogs; these dogs were more likely to die. See SY10.

tests.finding: Below 3.3 mmol/L in 19.8% of admitted B. rossi dogs; odds ratio for death 3.5 [R21][R3].
tests.note: Measure in every collapsed dog, puppy, and dog with severe anaemia, vomiting or icterus. See SY16.

tests.finding: Above 0.55 L/L (55%): 3 of 4 dogs died. Below 0.15 L/L (15%): 14% died [R3].
tests.note: Haemoconcentration is a worse sign than anaemia. See SY14 and SY01.

tests.finding: Capillary parasitaemia is higher than venous; both were higher in B. rossi dogs that died [R16].
tests.note: Parasitaemia did not differ by outcome in a small B. canis series [R22].

tests.test: Blood lactate (hand-held meter or blood gas)
tests.finding: Admission above 5.0 mmol/L, above 2.5 mmol/L at 8 to 24 h, or a fall of less than 50% within 8 to 16 h were linked to death in 90 B. rossi dogs [R8].
tests.note: All 8 B. canis non-survivors were hyperlactataemic [R22].

tests.test: Complete blood count with manual differential
tests.finding: Band neutrophils above 0.5 x10^9/L: odds ratio for death 4.9 in B. rossi [R3]. Leukopenia below 6 x10^9/L and monocytopenia below 0.2 x10^9/L marked SIRS in B. canis [R11].
tests.note: Leukopenia was found in B. canis non-survivors [R22].

tests.test: Urea, creatinine, bilirubin, ALT, ALP, CK
tests.finding: Compare with the organ criteria. Urea above 14 mmol/L and bilirubin above 14.7 µmol/L separated non-survivors in B. rossi [R3].
tests.note: The organ criteria come from B. canis [R2].

tests.finding: Refractory hypotension with MODS defined septic shock, which was fatal in all 10 dogs [R14].
High cortisol and ACTH, and low T4, were linked to death; cut-offs cortisol above 388 nmol/L and T4 below 4.8 nmol/L [R17][R3].
tests.note: B. rossi. Results come too late for triage.

differentials.distinguish: Measure glucose before calling a comatose dog a case of cerebral babesiosis [R21].

differentials.condition: Bacterial sepsis or another cause of SIRS
differentials.distinguish: SIRS criteria are not specific, and the consensus does not recommend them to identify sepsis [R6]. Look for a source of infection.
PCR. The Onderstepoort prognostic studies excluded these dogs [R17][R3].
In Hungary, DIC predicted MODS better than SIRS (6 of 11 against 5 of 22 dogs) [R12]. See SY03.
Count the failing organs; the outcome worsens with each organ added [R4][R12].

grading.criteria: No organ dysfunction [R2]. Mortality 3% in Hungary [R12].
One organ dysfunction. Mortality 21% in Hungary [R12].
Two or more organs. Mortality 67% in Hungary [R12]; survival 45%, 10% and 0% with two, three and four organs in Croatia [R4].
MODS with refractory hypotension. 10 of 86 admissions; all died [R14].
A score from admission markers, among them urea, ALT and lactate; cut-off 0.141, sensitivity 79%, specificity 83% in 108 dogs. Not validated elsewhere [R18].

approach.detail: Look for collapse, cerebral signs, abnormal breathing and a poor circulation. These dogs die more often, and most deaths are in the first 24 hours [R3][R1][R16].

approach.action: Measure glucose and haematocrit at once
approach.detail: Treat hypoglycaemia (SY16) and life-threatening anaemia (SY01). A normal or high haematocrit with haemolysis is a danger sign (SY14) [R21][R3].

approach.action: Start antibabesial treatment and standard support
approach.detail: Onderstepoort standard care was diminazene, red cell or whole blood transfusion and IV fluids as needed [R3]. Drugs and doses are in TX00.
Check creatinine, urea, bilirubin, ALT, CK, breathing and mentation against the criteria. Look for organ dysfunction; do not rely on SIRS [R2][R6].

approach.action: Measure lactate again at 8 and 16 hours
approach.detail: A lactate that stays above 2.5 mmol/L, or falls by less than half, was linked to death [R8].
Refer dogs with two or more failing organs, refractory hypotension, cerebral signs or lung oedema. Survival falls with each organ added, and septic shock was fatal in every reported dog [R4][R14].

approach.action: Treat each organ on its own page
approach.detail: Kidney SY05, liver SY06, brain SY07, lung SY08, heart SY09, shock SY10, pancreas SY12, coagulation SY03. No drug against the inflammatory response has shown benefit [R9][R10].

treatments.name: Supportive intensive care, organ by organ
treatments.aim: Keep oxygen delivery and organ function while the antibabesial drug acts.
treatments.evidence_summary: Large cohorts describe this care but did not test it against no care. In 320 B. rossi dogs, care was diminazene, transfusion and IV fluids, with complications treated at the clinician's choice; 10.6% died [R3]. In 40 B. canis dogs, complicated cases received IV fluids, oxygen, analgesia and antibiotics [R2].
treatments.cautions: The doses for each organ support are on the organ pages.
treatments.monitoring: Glucose, haematocrit and lactate at admission, 8 and 16 h; organ criteria daily [R8][R21].

treatments.name: Antibiotics for suspected secondary bacterial infection
treatments.aim: Treat a bacterial infection added to babesiosis.
treatments.evidence_summary: In one Zagreb study, 7 of 11 B. canis dogs with complications received IV antibiotics. The study took leukocytes above 17 x10^9/L, or neutropenia with lymphopenia, as a sign of secondary infection. The outcome with and without antibiotics was not compared [R2]. No study of blood cultures in dogs with babesiosis was found.

doses.context: B. canis, complicated cases, 1 cohort (Zagreb), with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid
doses.note: Dose and frequency as the source states them; check against a formulary.

treatments.cautions: SIRS criteria do not show that an infection is bacterial [R6].
treatments.monitoring: Leukocyte count and differential; the source of infection.

treatments.name: Plasmapheresis (extracorporeal blood purification)
treatments.aim: Remove circulating mediators and toxins in dogs with multiple organ failure.
treatments.evidence_summary: Russian reports only. A 2026 study added plasmapheresis to imidocarb and reported faster recovery and better renal, hepatic and cardiovascular function; the abstract gives no number of dogs and no design [R23]. In a series of 12 dogs in St Petersburg, one dog improved only after plasmapheresis [R24]. Neither report is controlled.
treatments.cautions: Needs extracorporeal equipment; a referral procedure.

treatments.name: N-acetylcysteine
treatments.evidence_summary: Two small randomised trials in B. gibsoni dogs given doxycycline, clindamycin and metronidazole. In 24 outpatient dogs, anaemia, the acute phase response and liver injury improved earlier with NAC [R19]. In 12 dogs, only antioxidant capacity and MCHC differed significantly [R20]. Neither trial was in dogs with SIRS or MODS, or in B. rossi.

doses.context: B. gibsoni, 12 of 24 outpatient dogs, randomised trial
B. gibsoni, 6 of 12 dogs, randomised trial

treatments.cautions: Not tested in critically ill dogs with babesiosis.
treatments.monitoring: Haematocrit, ALT and CRP, as in the trials [R19].

treatments.name: Pentoxifylline
treatments.aim: Block TNF production and improve capillary blood flow.
treatments.evidence_summary: No study in dogs. Human falciparum malaria only: two randomised trials found shorter coma in cerebral malaria [R25][R26]; two other randomised trials found no clinical benefit, and one stopped early, with more nausea on the drug [R27][R28].
treatments.cautions: No canine dose for this use was found; human doses are not given here.

treatments.name: Glucocorticoids against the inflammatory response
treatments.evidence_summary: No study in dogs with babesiosis tested them for SIRS or MODS; the 320-dog B. rossi cohort excluded dogs given anti-inflammatory drugs in the previous 4 weeks [R3]. In human cerebral malaria, high-dose dexamethasone prolonged coma and more than doubled complications [R9]. A Cochrane review of two trials found no benefit [R10].
treatments.cautions: More gastrointestinal bleeding and pneumonia with dexamethasone in human cerebral malaria [R9]. Their use in secondary IMHA is a separate question: see SY02.

prognosis.text: Overall, 10.6% of 320 B. rossi dogs died or were euthanased, and treated dogs that died did so within 24 hours [R3]. In B. canis, mortality rose from 3% without complications to 21% with one and 67% with several [R12]. No single finding or score is validated as a decision rule: the cut-offs were set on the dogs they describe, and multivariable analysis found no independent predictor [R3].

indicators.meaning: All 6 B. rossi dogs died [R3]; CNS involvement gave a 57 times greater chance of death in an earlier cohort [R5].
Five times the risk of death (B. rossi) [R5]; creatinine above 106 µmol/L, odds ratio 7.6 [R3].
Odds ratio for death 3.5 (B. rossi) [R3]; also linked to death in an earlier cohort [R8].

indicators.finding: Lactate above 5.0 mmol/L on admission, or not falling
indicators.meaning: Linked to death; persistently above 4.4 mmol/L was a very poor sign (B. rossi) [R8].
Linked to death in two Onderstepoort studies, which may share dogs [R17][R3].
B. canis survival 45%, 10% and 0% with two, three and four organs [R4].
Not linked to death in B. rossi [R5][R3].

related.why: Secondary immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia, where glucocorticoids are a separate question.
Acute kidney injury, the commonest organ in MODS.
Acute lung injury, ARDS and pulmonary oedema.

evidence_gaps: No trial in dogs with B. rossi or B. canis has tested any treatment aimed at the inflammatory response.
No study of NSAIDs, vitamins C or E, pentoxifylline or fresh frozen plasma in dogs with babesiosis was found.
No study of blood cultures was found, so it is not known how often bacterial sepsis accompanies babesiosis.
No admission cut-off or score has been tested prospectively in a new group of dogs.
The SIRS and organ criteria differ between research groups; there is no common definition of complicated babesiosis.
The Onderstepoort cohorts may share dogs, so the number of independent B. rossi studies is uncertain.
MODS data for B. gibsoni and B. vogeli are scarce, and no validation of canine illness severity scores (such as APPLE) in babesiosis was found in this run.

search.note: Searched the local review (combined set, SEV synthesis, notes) and PubMed and Europe PMC for SIRS, MODS, prognosis and each candidate treatment, with human malaria trials for glucocorticoids and pentoxifylline. Welzl 2001 and Matijatko 2010 were read as abstracts only. Mechanistic marker studies were left out.
